messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas is a 45-year-old journalist who has spent the better part of two decades reporting from conflict zones. He is married to Linda, a high school teacher, and they live in a quiet suburb of Chicago. Eight months ago, while on assignment in a Middle Eastern country, he was kidnapped by a militia group and held captive for eleven days. He was blindfolded, bound at the wrists and neck with rough rope, and kept in a windowless room. His captors were often drunk; the sour smell of alcohol clung to their breath and clothes, and it filled the small space whenever they came to interrogate or taunt him. They touched him frequently—shoving him, grabbing his collar, sometimes patting him down roughly. The neck pain from the rope burn never fully healed, and the ache has become a constant companion.

Back home, Thomas tried to resume his normal life, but the world no longer felt safe. The first time Linda reached out to touch his shoulder from behind, he flinched and jerked away so violently that she stumbled. He saw the hurt in her eyes but could not explain that the sensation of an unexpected hand on his body sent him straight back to that room. He began sleeping on the couch, partly because Linda’s accidental brushing against him at night would trigger a jolt of terror, and partly because the silence of the bedroom was too easily broken by his own hypervigilant scanning for footsteps or voices. He stopped going to the neighborhood bar with friends; even the faintest trace of beer on someone’s breath made his stomach clench and his heart race.

At work, Thomas took a desk job reviewing wire copy, but the newsroom was a minefield. The sudden ring of a telephone or the crackle of a loudspeaker announcement would make him drop what he was holding and scan the room for exits. He started wearing noise-canceling headphones, but even then, he was on guard, waiting for the next unexpected sound. A dropped metal tray in the office cafeteria once sent him diving under a table, his hands covering his head, while colleagues stared in shock. He told himself he was overreacting, but the feeling of imminent danger was so visceral that he could not talk himself out of it. He was certain that any loud noise could mean the captors had found him, that the worst was happening again.

The memory of the captivity played over and over in his mind like a film he could not turn off. It would intrude in the middle of a conversation, a shower, or while he was trying to sleep—always with the same raw terror he had felt when the ropes first tightened around his neck. The images were fragmented but vivid: the smell of cheap liquor, the sting of rope burn, the feeling of a hand grabbing his collar. He had come to believe that he was broken, that his body and mind would never stop reacting to a threat that was no longer there.

The breaking point came two weeks ago when a car backfired outside the grocery store, and Thomas dropped to the pavement, curled into a ball, shouting for his captors to stop. Linda had to help him up and drive him home. That night, she told him gently that he could not keep living this way. He agreed to see a therapist, though he was afraid—afraid that talking about the memory would make it stronger, afraid that he would never feel safe again, and afraid that the man he used to be was already gone. Part of him hoped that someone could help him put the film on pause, even for a while.
